name: 04-performance
title: Scalable Simulation — performance, acceleration, and fidelity-aware execution
question:
How fast is the simulation core, and where does the compute go? For one matched
48 h sepsis run, what does each engine cost, what dominates that cost, and how much
does the learned surrogate save?
objective:
Profile the compute across engines on one matched run: the full-run wall-clock
(BioGears, Tellurium), the dominant cost (the stiff ODE integration), whether a
faster integrator helps, and the surrogate's per-step speedup. A live, reproducible
micro-benchmark sits behind the full-run numbers.
claim:
For one matched 48 h severe-sepsis run, the same spec spans more than 4 orders of
magnitude of compute. BioGears (C++ physiology) takes ~3.38 h. Tellurium (exact SBML
via roadrunner/CVODE) takes ~2.81 h. The PyTorch surrogate takes ~0.2 s — about
40,000x faster than the exact SBML path. The exact engines spend nearly all of that
time integrating the stiff 91-state ODE. That solve needs an implicit stiff solver
(CVODE), so a faster or Rust explicit integrator cannot speed it up; the real levers
are a better stiff solver, GPU-parallel patients, or a surrogate. The surrogate
replaces the ODE solve with one forward pass. A live per-step micro-benchmark on this
machine measures ~526 ms for one exact CVODE step of the real model against ~0.04 ms
for one surrogate forward pass — the exact per-step cost is ~13,000x the surrogate's.
The surrogate is a fast approximate tier (bounded, not yet clinically accurate), not
a drop-in replacement.

expected_behavior.name: stiff-ode-is-the-bottleneck

expected_behavior.name: rust-backend-runs-the-same-composite
expected_behavior.statement: The same sepsis composite runs under the Rust viva-core execution backend and reproduces the process-bigraph Python result (determinism); the engine swap moves framework overhead, not the stiff solve.

expected_behavior.statement: Acceleration is only useful where predictions stay admissible: on the severe arm the surrogate leaves physical bounds for 8 of 9 observables, so it is screening-grade at best and the exact engine is required.

findings.summary: One 48 h run, three engines, 4+ orders of magnitude of compute.
findings.detail:
Matched 48 h severe-sepsis run of the same spec (BioGears + Tellurium from the
committed engine-runtime study; surrogate from the folded-in surrogate work):
  - BioGears 8.2.0 (C++ physiology): ~3.38 h
  - Tellurium exact SBML (roadrunner CVODE): ~2.81 h
  - PyTorch surrogate (576-step rollout): ~0.2 s (~40,000x faster than exact)
The two exact engines are the same order of magnitude and both dominated by the
stiff 91-state ODE solve. The surrogate skips the solve entirely (one forward
pass per step), at the cost of accuracy.
findings.statement: The 4+ order-of-magnitude compute spread is a real, matched-spec measurement, but it is about cost alone. The surrogate's ~40,000x full-run and ~13,000x per-step speedups matter only once the fidelity gate is met. Whether the surrogate is a drop-in replacement is decided in study 05, not here.
findings.explanation:
Three engines run the same 48 h severe-sepsis spec and split into two groups. The two exact engines (BioGears ~3.38 h, Tellurium ~2.81 h) sit within the same order of magnitude because both spend their time on the same stiff 91-state ODE solve. The PyTorch surrogate (~0.2 s) sits four orders below because it replaces that solve with a single forward pass. The live per-step micro-benchmark (~526 ms for one exact CVODE step vs ~0.04 ms for one surrogate pass, ~13,000x) pins the cost to that solve, so the spread comes from mechanism, not measurement noise. The companion finding rules out a faster integrator: the ODE is stiff, so an explicit method is unstable and wrong on the fast cardiovascular states.

This study sits downstream of composition -> ensembles -> workflows. It inherits the spec, the matched run, and the engine wrappers rather than re-deriving them, and it feeds fidelity (study 05). It measures cost under a fixed spec and does not measure correctness.

The speedups are compute-only. They tell you which engine is cheaper, not whether the surrogate can replace the exact SBML path. That question is answered by a different number, held-out trajectory error against the exact engine, which study 05's fidelity validator measures. Until that validator passes, the surrogate is a fast approximate tier. The claim this study supports is narrow: the bottleneck is the stiff solve, and the surrogate removes it, at a cost in accuracy this study does not quantify.

findings.summary: The bottleneck is the stiff ODE solve — a faster integrator is not a lever.
findings.detail:
The sepsis ODE is stiff, so only one solver class works: an implicit stiff method
(CVODE/BDF), already compiled as C inside libroadrunner. An explicit fixed-step
integrator (the kind a from-scratch Rust engine uses) is unstable on the real
model and wrong on the fast cardiovascular states, even at ~173 M steps per 48 h.
Rewriting the integrator in another language is not the speed lever. The levers
are a better or warm-started stiff solver, GPU-parallel patients, or a surrogate.
The composition engine is interchangeable on its own: the SBML composite is
bit-identical under process-bigraph Python and the viva-core Rust engine, so that
swap moves only framework overhead.

findings.summary: The Rust viva-core backend runs the same sepsis composite and reproduces the Python result (within-tolerance).
findings.detail:
The composition engine is interchangeable independently of the solver. We ran the
identical sepsis composite under process-bigraph (Python) and under the Rust
viva-core backend (run_rust_backend.py -> rust_backend.json, 60 ticks × 10 s,
healthy baseline). The two backends agree within tolerance: blood pathogen and
tissue integrity are bit-identical, and the hemodynamic observables match to ~1e-5
(max abs diff ~6.6e-5 on SBP). The ~1e-5 residual is roadrunner's
cold-start-vs-warm effect, not an engine disagreement. Wall-clock: Python ~24.0 s
vs viva-core ~21.4 s (ratio ~1.12). This is an execution-backend swap. Roadrunner
does the stiff ODE math in both, so viva-core just runs the composite graph
(state, scheduling, emit) around the same solver. On a single heavy stiff process
the wall-clock difference is framework overhead, not a faster stiff solve.
viva-core's per-tick advantage shows up on many-process or many-tick composites,
and the stiff solve itself stays fixed (see the stiff-ODE finding). What this arm
shows is backend interchangeability and determinism: same composite, two execution
engines, the same numbers.

findings.summary: Live per-step micro-benchmark: the stiff solve is ~13,000x the surrogate forward pass.
findings.detail:
Reproducible on this machine (bench_live.py, warm): one exact CVODE step of the
real 91-state sepsis model costs ~526 ms, against ~0.04 ms for one surrogate
forward pass — the exact per-step solve is ~13,000x the surrogate's. This is the
per-step view behind the full-run wall-clocks, and it shows directly where the
compute goes: the stiff ODE solve. The surrogate is a fast approximate tier (see
study 05 for the fidelity picture).

findings.summary: Speed without admissibility: on severe sepsis the surrogate leaves physical bounds for 8 of 9 observables.
findings.detail:
Acceleration is only useful where the predictions are admissible. Checking the
committed surrogate severe-arm trajectory (data/real_trajectories.json, at the
surrogate's trained 300 s timestep) against simple physical bounds
(surrogate_admissibility.py -> surrogate_admissibility.json, chart 04): 8 of 9
observables leave admissible ranges. The surrogate reaches MAP ~ -158 mmHg, tissue
integrity ~ -6.1, and negative blood pathogen — all physically impossible. Only SVR
stays in bounds. So on severe sepsis the surrogate is not admissible, let alone
mechanistically accurate: its ~40,000x speed does not help here, and the exact
engine is required. This draws the honest line the performance story needs —
screening-grade speed is only a benefit inside the regime where the surrogate stays
physical. A fair held-out-severity admissibility protocol at the trained timestep is
the pending validator (study 07, criterion SURR-01).
